big: Fund P grew 29% a year over the last three years. Fund Q managed 13%. An adviser who stops at that line recommends P. An adviser who rolls the window sees why that can be a mistake.

lines: Fund P gave 29% a year for the last three years. Why would I not just buy that one?
A three-year return depends on which three years you pick. Let us slide the window along the whole record and watch.

alt: Bars showing what 100 rupees became in fund P over eight different three-year windows
caps: Made-up star fund P. Each bar is what ₹100 became over three years, for a window ending that year.
Windows ending in years 3 to 5 gave ₹113, ₹113 and a loss, ₹94.
Only the last window shows ₹216. A pitch picks the best end date and calls it the record.
Rolling windows show the whole range, not the flattering corner.

alt: Bars comparing star fund P and steady fund Q on the latest window, the median window and the share of windows beating the benchmark
caps: Now roll a three-year window one month at a time across ten years: 85 windows.
On the latest window P wins easily. The typical window says otherwise: P 5.8%, Q 10.1%.
Windows beating the benchmark: P 28%, which is 24 of 85. Q 79%, which is 67 of 85.
Repeatable beats spectacular. One hot streak is not yet a process.

h: A ₹10,000 SIP over the same ten years
intro: Lump-sum return a year, and SIP XIRR a year, on made-up paths.
note: P's late surge hit a SIP corpus that had already grown, so its XIRR looks far better than its lump sum. XIRR also depends on the end date.

q: A pitch says Fund P returned 29% a year over three years against 12.6% for its benchmark. Rolling returns over ten years show P beat the benchmark in only 24 of 85 three-year windows. What is the fair reading?
opts: P's record is excellent, since the latest window matters most
P has failed, because it lost to the benchmark in most windows
P's edge rests on a late burst, so one window flatters it
The 85 windows prove that P's average return is below 5%
why: Recency is one window. The same ten years show P behind its benchmark in about seven windows out of every ten.
P still ended ahead over ten years, so failed overreaches. Its edge is concentrated in one stretch, not absent.
The headline sits on its best window. Rolling shows the gains came in one stretch, so repeatability is unproven.
Window counts show how often P won, not its average. P's median window was 5.8%, a different figure altogether.

q: A rival says Fund Z beat its benchmark in 80% of 85 rolling 3-year windows from ten years of monthly data, so that is 68 independent wins. What is wrong with that claim?
opts: Windows overlap; ten years hold about three separate spans
Rolling windows can only be built from yearly data, never monthly
Eighty percent is too low a share to count as consistent
Three-year windows are meaningless; only one-year windows count
why: Each window shares 35 of its 36 months with its neighbour, so the 68 wins are near-copies and the evidence is thin.
Monthly steps are normal practice. The weakness of the count is overlap, not the size of the step between windows.
A high share is useful, but the number of independent spans matters more than the percentage the windows produce.
Three-year windows suit many investors' holding periods. The issue is how many separate spans exist, not their length.

q: Over the same ten years, Fund P shows a lump-sum return of 11.4% a year but an SIP XIRR of 14.4%. The benchmark shows 10.6% and 10.2%. Why is P's SIP figure so much higher?
opts: SIPs always earn more than lump sums in every fund and market
P charges lower costs to SIP investors than to lump-sum ones
XIRR counts each instalment at its own date, so it is overstated
P surged late, when a big SIP corpus was already invested
why: SIP and lump sum differ with the path. A fund that falls late would show the reverse, so no such rule exists.
Costs are charged on the fund, not on how the money arrived. SIP and lump-sum holders pay the same expense ratio.
XIRR dates each instalment, which is the correct way to measure a SIP. The gap comes from when the gains arrived.
A late surge hits every unit bought so far, so SIP XIRR rises more. It still depends on the end date, so check rolling.

q: A client will invest for at least seven years. Fund R beat its benchmark in 88% of rolling 1-year windows but only 52% of rolling 5-year windows. Which figure should guide the choice?
opts: The 1-year figure, as it has far more windows to learn from
The 5-year figure, since it matches her holding period
The better of the two, which shows what the fund can do
The average of the two, which gives a balanced overall view
why: One-year windows are noisier and reflect luck as much as skill. A client holding for seven years lives through longer windows.
Match the window to the holding period. For a seven-year investor, the 5-year result is closest to what she will experience.
Choosing the better number is the cherry-picking that rolling returns are meant to stop, now done across window lengths.
Averaging mixes two horizons and fits neither. Choose the window first, from the client's holding period, then read it.

pts: A point-to-point return depends on its dates. Roll the window to see every start and end.
Read the share of rolling windows beating the benchmark, using a window as long as the client's holding period.
Overlapping windows are not independent wins, and SIP XIRR depends on the end date too.
